lead: A regulated DC supply must hold its output steady when the input and the load change. A linear regulator does this by placing a transistor in series and burning the extra voltage as heat. A switched-mode power supply instead chops the input at high frequency, stores energy in an inductor or transformer, and filters the result. The first is simple and quiet but wasteful; the second reaches 70–95 % efficiency and is used in phone chargers, laptop adapters and LED drivers. This chapter compares both and shows where the heat goes.
prereq: You need the MOSFET switch and heat-sink ideas from Unit 1, the rectifier and capacitor filter from Unit 2, and the chopper idea from Chapter 3.1.

sections.h3: Linear regulator: a controlled voltage drop

blocks.text: A linear regulator keeps V<sub>o</sub> fixed by using a series pass transistor as a variable resistor. The transistor, often a BJT Darlington or a MOSFET, stays in its active (linear) region, never fully on or off. An error amplifier compares a fraction βV<sub>o</sub> of the output (β is the divider ratio, below 1) with a zener or bandgap reference V<sub>ref</sub>. It drives the pass device so βV<sub>o</sub> ≈ V<sub>ref</sub>. If V<sub>o</sub> falls, the error amplifier turns the pass device on harder and reduces its voltage drop.

The input must stay above V<sub>o</sub> by the dropout voltage, the minimum across the pass device that still allows control. Below dropout the regulator shuts down or loses regulation. A low-dropout (LDO) type uses a pass device with a small dropout, often under 0.5 V. A shunt regulator places the control device across the load instead; it is simple but wastes more current.
η = (V<sub>o</sub>·I<sub>o</sub>) / [V<sub>in</sub>·(I<sub>o</sub> + I<sub>q</sub>)] ≈ V<sub>o</sub> / V<sub>in</sub> ; P<sub>d</sub> = (V<sub>in</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>) · I<sub>o</sub>
blocks.where: η is efficiency (fraction); V<sub>o</sub> is output voltage (V); V<sub>in</sub> is input voltage (V); I<sub>o</sub> is load current (A); I<sub>q</sub> is quiescent current (A); P<sub>d</sub> is heat in the pass device (W). The approximation holds when I<sub>q</sub> is much smaller than I<sub>o</sub>.

blocks.text: The dissipation P<sub>d</sub> sets the heat-sink size using the thermal design of Unit 1. A 5 V, 1 A load from 12 V makes 7 W of heat, so a small plastic package overheats without a heatsink. Linear regulators suit low-current, low-noise analogue circuits and post-regulation after a switcher.

A switched-mode power supply (SMPS) takes AC mains through a rectifier and capacitor filter to a rough DC bus. A high-frequency switch then chops this DC into pulses. A transformer gives isolation and a voltage step; in non-isolated types an inductor stores energy. An output rectifier and L-C filter smooth the pulses. A PWM controller changes the duty ratio D, the on-time fraction, to hold V<sub>o</sub> fixed.

items: Rectify and filter the mains to a DC bus.
Chop the DC bus with a high-frequency switch.
Transfer energy through a transformer or inductor.
Rectify and L-C filter the pulses.
Feed back V<sub>o</sub> through an optocoupler or auxiliary winding to the PWM controller.

blocks.text: Loss is mostly conduction loss I²R in the switch, winding and diode, plus switching loss from voltage-current overlap at every transition. Good designs reach η = 70–95 %. Higher switching frequency f<sub>s</sub> shrinks the transformer and inductor because the volt-second (flux) swing per cycle is smaller, so fewer turns and a smaller core are needed; it raises switching loss and EMI. Phone chargers, laptop bricks and LED drivers use f<sub>s</sub> from tens of kHz to a few hundred kHz.
η = P<sub>o</sub> / P<sub>in</sub> ; P<sub>loss</sub> = P<sub>in</sub> − P<sub>o</sub>
blocks.where: P<sub>o</sub> is output power (W); P<sub>in</sub> is input power (W); P<sub>loss</sub> is loss as heat (W); η is efficiency (fraction).

blocks.text: The price is output ripple, electromagnetic interference (EMI), and a control loop that must stay stable. Layout, snubbers and input filters become part of the design. See Chapter 3.3 for the buck cell and Chapter 3.6 for isolated types.

Use a linear regulator when the drop is small, the current is low, and quiet output matters. Use an SMPS when the input-output difference is large, the current is high, or isolation is needed. The table summarises the trade-off for 12 V to 5 V at 1 A.

The 7 W and 0.88 W are from the worked example below. A switcher can step up as well as down, so its efficiency must use P<sub>o</sub>/P<sub>in</sub>, not V<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>in</sub>. Do not size a linear heatsink from V<sub>o</sub>·I<sub>o</sub>.

figure.caption: Two paths from a 12 V DC input to a 5 V load: the pass transistor drops the excess as heat, while the high-frequency switch and small transformer pass energy in pulses. Notice the shared output filter and load.

spec.title: Two ways to drop 12 V to 5 V
spec.aria: A block diagram shows AC mains through a rectifier and filter to a 12 V DC bus, then two parallel paths: a pass transistor that burns excess voltage and a high-frequency switch with transformer, both feeding an output filter and load.

examples.question: A 5 V linear regulator takes 1 A from a 12 V input. (a) Find the pass-transistor dissipation and the efficiency. (b) A switched-mode supply of 85 % efficiency does the same job; find its input power, its loss, and the ratio of the linear loss to the SMPS loss.
steps: Voltage across the pass device = V<sub>in</sub> − V<sub>o</sub> = 12 V − 5 V = 7 V.
P<sub>loss</sub> = P<sub>in</sub> − P<sub>o</sub> = 5.88 W − 5 W = 0.88 W (0.882 W before rounding).
Ratio = 7 W / 0.8824 W = 7.93 (about eight times); the division uses the unrounded loss.
examples.answer: The linear regulator heats the pass device by 7 W at 41.7 % efficiency; the SMPS draws 5.88 W and loses 0.88 W, so the linear regulator's loss is 7.93 times the SMPS loss.
examples.check:
Vo = 5.0
Vin = 12.0
Io = 1.0
eta_smps = 0.85
Pd = (Vin - Vo) * Io
eta_lin = Vo / Vin * 100
Po = Vo * Io
Pin = Po / eta_smps
loss = Pin - Po
ratio = Pd / loss
print(round(Pd, 1))
print(round(eta_lin, 1))
print(round(Po, 1))
print(round(Pin, 2))
print(round(loss, 2))
print(round(ratio, 2))

traps: Linear-regulator loss is (V<sub>in</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>)·I<sub>o</sub>, not V<sub>in</sub>·I<sub>o</sub>. Using V<sub>in</sub>·I<sub>o</sub> counts the useful output power as heat.
SMPS efficiency is P<sub>o</sub>/P<sub>in</sub>. V<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>in</sub> is meaningless for a switcher, which can step up or step down.
Dropout is a voltage difference, not a current. Below V<sub>o</sub> + dropout the regulator cannot hold regulation.
A higher switching frequency shrinks the magnetics but does not automatically raise efficiency; switching loss and EMI grow.

quiz.q: In a series linear regulator, which device drops the excess voltage, and in which region does it operate?
quiz.a: The series pass transistor drops the excess voltage. It operates in its active (linear) region.

quiz.q: Why does an LDO need a smaller input-output difference than a standard linear regulator?
quiz.a: Its pass device has a lower dropout voltage, so the minimum V<sub>in</sub> − V<sub>o</sub> needed for control is smaller.

quiz.q: A 9 V input feeds a 5 V linear regulator at 0.5 A. Find the pass-device dissipation and the efficiency.
An SMPS has P<sub>o</sub> = 24 W and P<sub>in</sub> = 30 W. Find its efficiency and loss. Why is V<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>in</sub> not its efficiency?
quiz.a: η = 24/30 = 0.80 = 80 %. Loss = 30 − 24 = 6 W. A switcher can step up or down, so voltage ratio does not equal power ratio; efficiency must use P<sub>o</sub>/P<sub>in</sub>.

quiz.q: State two reasons why increasing SMPS switching frequency shrinks the transformer.
quiz.a: (1) Each cycle must handle less energy, so the core can be smaller. (2) The volt-second product per cycle falls, so fewer turns are needed. Filter components also shrink, but that is separate from the transformer.

quiz.q: A linear regulator and an SMPS both deliver 5 V, 2 A from 12 V. The SMPS is 88 % efficient. Compare their heat.
quiz.a: Linear: P<sub>d</sub> = (12 − 5) V × 2 A = 14 W. SMPS: P<sub>o</sub> = 10 W, P<sub>in</sub> = 10/0.88 = 11.36 W, loss = 1.36 W. The linear regulator makes about 10.3 times more heat.

quiz.q: Name two elements used to give isolated feedback in an SMPS.
quiz.a: An optocoupler and an auxiliary winding on the transformer.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production supplies are usually integrated power-management ICs with the switch, controller and protection on one die. Digital control can adjust loop gain and report fault data. Wide band-gap devices such as GaN allow higher switching frequency and smaller adapters, at tighter EMI layout cost. Search for 'LDO dropout', 'flyback optocoupler feedback' and 'conducted EMI'.
